title: Canada's information ecosystem is age-stratified and misinformation-saturated, making trust and detection capacity part of civic infrastructure
source_unit: Statistics Canada, Canadian Social Survey and Survey Series on People and Their Communities, 2026

observations.period: 2025 Canadian Social Survey; Canadians aged 15 and older

denominator.unit: Canadian Social Survey respondents aged 15 and older; exact analytic denominator not headlined in article overview

monthly_misinformation_exposure.unit: percent seeing suspected misleading, false or inaccurate information online at least monthly

difficulty_detecting_change.unit: percent saying it is harder to distinguish true from false information than three years earlier

misinformation_concern.unit: percent very or extremely concerned about online misinformation

observations.method: Canadian Social Survey measures of self-reported online exposure, concern and perceived ability to distinguish true from false information.
observations.uncertainty: Exposure and detection are self-reported perceptions; the survey wording cannot establish whether people saw more misinformation, recognized more of it or changed their reporting thresholds.
observations.counterinterpretation: High reported exposure may partly reflect heightened awareness of misinformation rather than a direct increase in objectively false content encountered.

denominator.unit: Canadian Social Survey respondents by age group; exact subgroup denominators not headlined in article overview

social_media_use_age_15_34.unit: percent of Canadians aged 15 to 34 identifying social media as a typical information source

social_media_use_age_75_plus.unit: percent of Canadians aged 75 and older

news_organization_use_age_75_plus.unit: percent of Canadians aged 75 and older

television_use_age_75_plus.unit: percent of Canadians aged 75 and older

observations.method: Cross-sectional comparison of typical information sources by age group.
observations.uncertainty: These are source-use patterns, not measures of source quality, attention time or persuasion; respondents can use multiple sources.
observations.subgroup: Canadians aged 15 to 24, 25 to 34 and 75 and older, with source comparisons across the full age distribution.
observations.counterinterpretation: Generational differences may reflect life stage, technology access, news habits and cohort effects rather than fixed age traits.

denominator.unit: Canadian Social Survey respondents by racialized identity; exact subgroup denominators not headlined in article overview

social_media_racialized.unit: percent of racialized Canadians identifying social media as a typical information source

news_organizations_racialized.unit: percent of racialized Canadians identifying news organizations as a typical information source

observations.method: Cross-sectional comparison of typical information sources by racialized identity.
observations.uncertainty: The categories aggregate diverse communities and do not identify platform mix, language, socioeconomic position or whether source use produces different misinformation exposure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Differences may be driven by age composition, language, migration history, community networks or access patterns rather than racialized identity itself.

denominator.unit: Canadian Social Survey respondents; exact analytic denominator not headlined in article overview

media_confidence_association.value: Higher confidence in media is associated with less reported difficulty distinguishing true from false information

interpersonal_social_trust_association.value: Higher interpersonal and social trust is also associated with greater confidence in distinguishing true from false information

observations.method: Survey association analysis relating confidence in media and interpersonal/social trust to perceived misinformation-detection difficulty.
observations.uncertainty: The relationship is observational and self-reported; trust may shape detection confidence, detection experiences may shape trust, or both may reflect education, media habits and broader institutional conditions.
observations.subgroup: Canadian Social Survey respondents, with comparisons by media confidence and social trust.
observations.counterinterpretation: Confidence in a trusted source can sometimes increase vulnerability to false information if trust is misplaced or insulated from correction.

related_sources.claim: Official Statistics Canada catalogue page for the article and downloadable publication.
Official PDF used for retrieval verification and hash.

boundary: This record adds a comparative information-ecosystem mechanism: misinformation exposure is widespread, source use is sharply age-stratified and racialized Canadians report a different source mix, while media confidence and social trust correlate with perceived detection ability. It is a Canadian cross-sectional/repeated-survey evidence base, not a causal estimate of misinformation effects, a behavioral trace of content exposure or a direct audit of truthfulness.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Statistics Canada article, catalogue page and downloadable PDF were retrieved and reviewed for exposure, concern, detection difficulty, information-source, age, racialized-identity and trust-association findings; the PDF was hashed.
